name: Barnum effect
statement: Given a personality description vague enough to fit almost anyone, people rate it as an accurate portrait of themselves in particular.
meaning: The trick is in a specific kind of vagueness. A Barnum statement is not empty; it is double-sided, so that whichever way a reader leans they can find themselves in it. Forer's eleventh item read "At times you are extroverted, affable, sociable, while at other times you are introverted, wary, reserved". That is true of everyone and reads as observant, because the reader supplies the half that applies and forgets the other half was there. The effect matters because it is the mechanism that keeps horoscopes, cold reading and unvalidated personality instruments in business: a client's feeling that a description fits is worthless as evidence that the instrument measures anything.

origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: Forer gave the 39 students of his introductory psychology class his Diagnostic Interest Blank, then a week later handed every one of them the same typed 13-statement sketch with the student's own name written on it. A footnote says the statements came largely from a newsstand astrology book. Asked to rate on a scale of zero, poor, to five, perfect, how far the sketch revealed basic characteristics of their personality, 16 gave a five and 18 a four, and five rated it below four. Paul Meehl proposed the label in 1956, crediting the underlying phrase to his colleague Donald G. Paterson, who called such writing "personality description after the manner of P. T. Barnum". Meehl quotes no words of Barnum's.

evidence: The paradigm has barely changed in seventy-five years, which is part of why it is so easy to run. Administer something that looks like an assessment, return identical feedback to everyone, and ask how well it describes them. Ratings come back high, and participants do not notice the sketch is generic until they see someone else's copy. Forer's class realised it when he read the first sketch item aloud and every hand went up. His students accepted 10.2 of the 13 statements as true on average, and they judged the test more kindly than the sketch: only one rating of the Diagnostic Interest Blank fell below four, against five for the sketch. Three weeks later he asked the 32 students then present to write down the ratings they remembered giving. Seven ratings of five came back as four and one as three, none rose, and Forer reports the fall as significant at the 1 per cent level. Three reviews of this literature were located: Snyder, Shenkel and Lowery in 1977, Dickson and Kelly in 1985, and Furnham and Schofield in 1987.

replication.headline: Repeated for decades with the same result, and a review of the literature reports that acceptance depends on how relevant and how flattering the description is.
replication.detail: Dickson and Kelly surveyed the research up to 1985 and concluded that acceptance of Barnum profiles turns on the relevance and the favourability of the profile, and to some extent on the type of assessment used. On favourability their tally runs one way. Sundberg's 1955 result was reproduced by five later studies, against a single study reporting equal acceptance of favourable and unfavourable sketches. That one measured acceptance through judges' ratings of participants' comments rather than the participants' own ratings, and two later studies corrected it. Both moderators point the same way. The effect is not a fixed rate of gullibility but a response to how personally addressed and how complimentary the description feels. That predicts where it will be largest, which is the condition a horoscope or a commercial personality report is written under. The favourability moderator has since been carried to chatbots. Pataranutaporn, Lee, Amores and Maes gave 238 participants pre-scripted predictions presented as the output of an AI, and report positive predictions rated more valid, personalised, reliable and useful than negative ones, by 36, 42, 27 and 22 per cent. Those four figures are quoted from their abstract, which is all of that paper this entry could obtain.

study.cite: Dickson, D. H., & Kelly, I. W. (1985). The 'Barnum effect' in personality assessment: A review of the literature. Psychological Reports, 57(2), 367-382.

limits: No meta-analysis with a pooled effect size was located. Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and OSF Registries were searched for this entry, and none holds a meta-analysis of the effect or a published multi-laboratory replication of it. OSF Registries holds three preregistrations, from 2020, 2025 and 2026, none of which carries a published result. The verdict here therefore rests on a narrative review published in 1985. Forer prints no mean rating of the sketch anywhere in his six pages, only the distribution; his one mean is the 10.2 items. Dickson and Kelly note that the majority of studies to that date used university students, which is close to the ideal conditions for the effect, and they recommend testing the general public instead. The effect also does not travel everywhere. Suwanaposee, Gutwin, Chen and Cockburn ran a crowd-sourced experiment with 492 participants on identical film recommendations for good and bad films, labelled either personalised or not. They report numerically lower mean quality scores for the personalised label, with no significant difference. Their own reading is that Barnum-like effects of personalisation have at most a small influence on perceived quality. That paper is described here from its abstract, because the publisher returned HTTP 403 to every attempt and no repository copy was found, so no test statistic and no analysed sample are quoted.
misreadings: Two different mean accuracy ratings circulate for Forer's class, and neither is in his paper. Robert Todd Carroll's Skeptic's Dictionary gives a class average of 4.26; the English Wikipedia article gives 4.30, on a scale it labels zero, very poor, to five, excellent, where Forer's own labels were poor and perfect. The quoted means are arithmetic performed on his Table 1 by later writers, and that table has two rows, one for ratings of the sketch and one for ratings of the test instrument, which are easy to confuse. This entry gives the distribution instead. The effect also gets described as proof that people are gullible, when the review's moderators say something more specific: acceptance rises when the description is favourable and when it appears tailored. That is closer to motivated reasoning about oneself than to general credulity. It is also frequently used as though it disproves personality assessment altogether. It does not; it shows that a client's endorsement cannot validate an instrument, which is an argument about what counts as evidence rather than about whether traits exist. And the effect is not confined to astrology: the same vulnerability applies to workplace personality profiles that are never checked against anything. Subjective validation, entry 231, names the mechanism proposed for these same experiments rather than a second body of evidence, so a page citing both in support of each other has counted one literature twice.
